slides.title: Chapter 14: Second-Layer Apps
slides.notes: This opening slide names the chapter and its question: what can be built on top of Bitcoin without changing its rules. The chapter covers the guarantees of the chain, colored coins, payment channels and the Lightning Network, which together make up the second layer. Every number you will meet on a result picture was computed with the chapter's own Python library or read from one recorded run of Bitcoin Core and lnd on private test chains. Mastering Bitcoin, third edition, chapter 14 is the source text, and the course page reruns every example.

slides.title: Today's route
slides.notes: The route has four parts, and they follow the order of the chapter: what the chain guarantees, colored coins and seals, payment channels, and the Lightning Network. Nineteen code examples and four true stories are spread across the parts. The examples are listed in the same order in the Run slide code menu of the course page, so each listing can be run and edited there. Use this slide to see where a topic sits in the whole route before you open its part.

slides.title: The questions this chapter answers
slides.notes: These seven questions are the chapter's own questions, rewritten so that each has an answer on a named slide. They run from the guarantees of the chain to the cost of a channel and the earnings of a relay. Read them first and try to answer each one from what you already know, then return to them in the summary slide at the end. A reader who can answer all seven has understood the chapter. The course page offers a quiz on the same questions.

slides.title: One chapter, four parts
slides.notes: The chapter has four parts, and this map shows how large each one is. The guarantees hold 24 key concepts and four examples, colored coins hold 8 concepts and two examples, payment channels hold 16 concepts and five examples, and Lightning holds 13 concepts and eight examples. Each part opens with a divider, followed by concept cards with literal meanings, code that runs, and in some parts a true story. Keep this map in mind: every later slide belongs to exactly one of the four boxes.

slides.title: What the chain guarantees
slides.notes: Bitcoin offers guarantees that any application can reuse: no double spend, immutability, a trusted timestamp and more. Software built on them is called a second-layer application, because it changes none of the chain's rules. The two columns name the two ideas of this part: the building blocks themselves, and applications such as a digital notary or a crowdfund that combine several of them. Four of the guarantees are tested on a private chain in the code slides that follow. For the full list see chapter 14 of Mastering Bitcoin.

slides.title: What the chain guarantees: concepts (1 of 4)
slides.notes: This slide defines 6 concepts of the part "What the chain guarantees". Applications from Building Blocks: Each application mixes several guarantees, as a digital notary mixes immutability, a timestamp and durability. Building Blocks (Primitives): The guarantees Bitcoin offers, which every application may reuse. Lighthouse: A crowdfunding application whose pledges are signed inputs, spendable only when the goal is met. Second-Layer Applications: Services built on Bitcoin's first layer that use its guarantees and change none of its rules. accounting: Outputs never exceed inputs, so a transaction cannot create or destroy value. auditability: Every transaction is public and links back to the genesis block. Retell each in your own words and connect it with the example slides of the part. The chapter text and the course page explain them in full.

slides.title: A double spend and the fee
slides.notes: No output can be spent twice in the same valid chain, and this slide shows how the network enforces it. Bitcoin Core, running on a private chain, accepted a first spend of one coin and refused a second spend that paid a lower fee, with a named reason in its reply. A second spend that paid a higher fee replaced the first one, and the first then vanished from the waiting pool. The bar chart shows the three fees in satoshis. This is example 1 in the Run slide code menu; related ideas are replace-by-fee in chapter 9.

slides.title: Two pizzas for 10,000 bitcoins
slides.notes: This true story dates the first purchase of a physical good with bitcoin. On 22 May 2010 the programmer Laszlo Hanyecz paid 10,000 bitcoins for two pizzas, after offering the coins in a forum post; a 19-year-old named Jeremy Sturdivant took the offer and ordered the pizzas from Papa John's in Jacksonville, Florida. The payment settled on the chain and waited for confirmations. That wait is why small everyday payments now travel through channels and the Lightning Network, which later slides explain. The link on the slide leads to the original forum thread.

slides.title: What the chain guarantees: concepts (2 of 4)
slides.notes: This slide defines 6 concepts of the part "What the chain guarantees". authorization: A script that asks for a signature cannot run without the holder of the private key. consistency: The deeper a block lies, the less likely it is to be reorganised. forgery protection: A transaction can spend only existing, validated outputs, so value cannot be counterfeited. immutability: The more work lies on top of a transaction, the more energy it takes to rewrite it. integrity: A signature covers the parts of a transaction it commits to, so they cannot be altered. neutrality: The network relays any valid transaction with a sufficient fee, whoever sends it. Retell each in your own words and connect it with the example slides of the part. The chapter text and the course page explain them in full.

slides.title: Nonexpiration and accounting
slides.notes: Two further guarantees are tested here. Nonexpiration means that a valid transaction stays valid for as long as its input is unspent: a transaction signed 150 blocks earlier was still accepted by the test node. Accounting means that outputs never exceed inputs, so a transaction cannot create value: one that paid out more than it took in was refused, whatever its signatures said, with the reason bad-txns-in-belowout. The table shows both results. Connect this slide with the concept cards on accounting and nonexpiration, and with example 2 of the Run slide code menu.

slides.title: What the chain guarantees: concepts (3 of 4)
slides.notes: This slide defines 6 concepts of the part "What the chain guarantees". no double spend: No output can be spent twice in the same valid chain of blocks. nonexpiration: A valid transaction stays valid for as long as its inputs are unspent. predictable issuance: Fewer than 21 million bitcoin will ever exist, issued at a known rate. primitives: The basic guarantees themselves, small enough to be combined in many ways. proof of existence: A document's hash in a transaction proves the document existed when that block was mined. quorum of control: A multisignature script demands a set number of keys, such as two of two. Retell each in your own words and connect it with the example slides of the part. The chapter text and the course page explain them in full.

slides.title: Proof of existence
slides.notes: Proof of existence is the guarantee that a hash in a transaction proves a document existed when the block holding it was mined. The code builds an output whose script is OP_RETURN followed by the hash of a document; such an output holds no value and nobody can spend it. The block gives the hash its date, here block 452, while the document itself never enters the chain. This is how a digital notary can be built from the guarantees of timestamping and immutability. It is example 3 in the Run slide code menu.
slides.new_title: Proof of existence with a hash

slides.title: What the chain guarantees: concepts (4 of 4)
slides.notes: This slide defines 6 concepts of the part "What the chain guarantees". recording external state: A transaction can commit to outside data through OP_RETURN or pay to contract. replication: Every full node keeps a copy of the chain, so the data survives local failures. second layer: A system that settles on the chain but does most of its work away from it. secure timestamping: The consensus rules keep block times roughly honest, so a recorded fact has a trusted date. timelock: A script clause can run only after a set time or block height. transaction atomicity: A transaction is mined in full or not at all, never halfway. Retell each in your own words and connect it with the example slides of the part. The chapter text and the course page explain them in full.

slides.title: Lighthouse: a crowdfund
slides.notes: Lighthouse is a crowdfunding application whose pledges are signed inputs that become spendable only when the goal is met. In the code, two pledges less the fee make the goal. One pledge alone is refused, because it pays out more than it takes in, and both together are accepted. Changing the output breaks the signatures, and a signature over every input and output stops a pledge that comes too late. The table lists four tries. This shows how the guarantees of authorization and integrity combine; see example 4 of the Run slide code menu.
slides.new_title: Lighthouse: a crowdfund on the chain

slides.title: Colored coins and seals
slides.notes: Colored coins are the second part of the chapter: a small amount of bitcoin is marked so that it stands for another asset, such as a share. Three ideas make that possible. A single-use seal is tied to an unspent output and opens only once, a public key can be tweaked so that it commits to a contract, and the receiver checks the whole history of the asset because the chain holds only commitments. Two of the three ideas are run in the code slides of this part. Chapter 14 of the book describes RGB and Taproot Assets.

slides.title: Colored coins and seals: concepts (1 of 2)
slides.notes: This slide defines 6 concepts of the part "Colored coins and seals". Client-Side Validation: The receiver checks the whole history of an asset; the chain holds only commitments. Colored Coins: A small amount of bitcoin is marked so that it stands for another asset, such as a share. Pay to Contract (P2C): A public key is tweaked so that it commits to a contract that nobody else sees. RGB: A colored coin protocol made to work with channels, built from seals, contracts and client checks. Single-Use Seals: A data structure that can be tied to another only once; an unspent output does that. Taproot Assets: A colored coin protocol, once called Taro, built around taproot-style contracts. Retell each in your own words; the course page explains them in full.

slides.title: Client-side validation
slides.notes: Client-side validation means the receiver checks the whole history of an asset, because the chain stores only commitments. The code builds the history of ACME tokens, which passes through two transactions and three outputs. Each step commits to its contract, and a forged contract does not match its commitment. Yet nothing in the chain shows that any token exists, so the receiver must read the history to know what the outputs mean. The table shows what the chain sees and what the receiver must verify. This is example 5 of the Run slide code menu.
slides.new_title: Client-side validation of a token history

slides.title: Colored coins and seals: concepts (2 of 2)
slides.notes: This slide defines 2 concepts of the part "Colored coins and seals". native forwarding: Every hop on a Lightning path must know the asset and hold a balance of it. translated forwarding: Only the first and last hops know the asset, and the hops between forward plain bitcoin. Retell each in your own words and connect it with the example slides of the part. The chapter text and the course page explain them in full.

slides.title: Pay to contract
slides.notes: Pay to contract tweaks a public key with a contract, so the key commits to an agreement that nobody else sees and looks like any other key. The code shows that a tweaked key gives a different address from the plain key. Revealing the contract and the tweak proves the commitment, a wrong contract fails the proof, and only the tweaked key can spend the output; the plain key cannot. Connect this with single-use seals and with taproot, where a similar tweak commits to a script tree. It is example 6 of the Run slide code menu.
slides.new_title: Pay to contract: a tweaked key

slides.title: Payment channels
slides.notes: Payment channels are the third part. Two people can trade many times and settle once, because only the funding and the settlement need to touch the chain. This part builds a channel step by step: a funding output that needs both keys, refunds with falling lock times, balances that move while capacity stays fixed, commitments that punish an old state, and a hash time lock that lets a secret claim a payment. Each step is run on a private chain with Bitcoin Core, and the chapter text gives the formal description.
slides.new_title: Payment channels: trade often, settle once

slides.title: Payment channels: key concepts (1 of 3)
slides.notes: This slide defines 6 concepts of the part "Payment channels". Asymmetric Revocable Commitments: Each side holds a commitment that delays its own payout and can be punished once it is old. Hash Time Lock Contracts (HTLC): A secret can claim the payment before a deadline, and the payer can reclaim it after. Making Trustless Channels: Signed refunds and lock times let each side leave safely without trusting the other. Payment Channels and State Channels: Two parties exchange signed transactions off the chain and settle on it later. Simple Payment Channel Example: Emma pays Fabian for each second of video, and a signed refund protects her. Spillman-style payment channel: A one-way channel of 2013: ever larger signed payments, and a refund behind a lock time. Retell each in your own words; the course page explains them in full.

slides.title: Emma and Fabian's channel
slides.notes: A payment channel starts with a funding output. In the example Emma funds one hour of video at 1,000 satoshis a second, which is 3,600,000 satoshis. The funding output is a two-of-two multisignature script, so spending it needs both signatures and Emma alone is refused. The witness script begins with the number 2 and ends with 2 and CHECKMULTISIG; in the table opcode 52 is OP_2 and ae is CHECKMULTISIG. This is the quorum-of-control guarantee at work, and example 7 of the Run slide code menu runs it.

slides.title: The first payment channels
slides.notes: This true story traces where payment channels came from. The Bitcoin Wiki and the first Bitcoin code describe an unrecorded transaction that could be replaced until its lock time. In April 2013 Mike Hearn posted about replacing transactions and Jeremy Spillman answered with a one-way channel design, in which the payer signs larger and larger payments while a refund waits behind a lock time. Hearn and Matt Corallo announced bitcoinj code in June 2013. Such channels were safe only with segwit transactions, which is why Emma signs her refund before sending the funding. The slide links to the sources.

slides.title: Payment channels: key concepts (2 of 3)
slides.notes: This slide defines 6 concepts of the part "Payment channels". State Channels - Basic Concepts and Terminology: A funding transaction opens the channel, commitments change it, and a settlement closes it. asymmetric commitment: The two commitments differ: the holder's own payout waits, the other side is paid at once. commitment transaction: A signed transaction that could be published but is held back and replaced by newer ones. funding transaction: The one transaction that locks the shared funds in a two-of-two output and opens the channel. payment channel: Two parties keep a running balance of signed transactions that they do not publish. preimage: The secret that hashes to the value in an HTLC; whoever knows it can claim the payment. Retell each in your own words; the course page explains them in full.

slides.title: Refunds with falling lock times
slides.notes: A channel needs a way out if the other party disappears, and this slide builds it. Emma signs six refunds before she funds the channel, each with a lower lock time than the one before, so the newest refund becomes valid first. At the start every refund is refused as not yet final. Six blocks before the newest lock time it is still refused, and five blocks before it is accepted. The table shows the six lock times. The idea combines the timelock guarantee with the earlier funding output. It is example 8 of the Run slide code menu.

slides.title: Payment channels: key concepts (3 of 3)
slides.notes: This slide defines 4 concepts of the part "Payment channels". refund transaction: A signed, time-locked transaction that returns the funds if the channel never starts. revocation key: A key of two secret halves that lets the wronged side take the whole channel after a cheat. settlement transaction: The final transaction that closes the channel and pays each side its share. state channel: The general form: any shared state is changed off the chain and secured by a final settlement. Retell each in your own words and connect it with the example slides of the part. The chapter text and the course page explain them in full.

slides.title: Balances move, capacity stays
slides.notes: The capacity of a channel is fixed when it is funded, and payments only move value between the two sides. In the example a channel of 100 units starts with everything on Alice's side. Each move shifts value to Bob, and the sum of the two balances stays at 100 after every step; the chart shows Alice's balance falling. A payment larger than the sender's balance cannot be made. This explains why a channel's capacity limits the largest payment it can carry, which matters again for routing in the Lightning part. It is example 9 of the Run slide code menu.

slides.title: On the chain, or off it?
slides.notes: A channel puts exactly two transactions on the chain: the funding transaction that opens it and the settlement that closes it for good. Everything between them stays off the chain as signed commitments that change the balances. No one else sees these updates and their fees are small. The chain acts as the court of last resort, which is why each side keeps its latest commitment and must be able to publish it. Compare the two columns and remember the rule: two transactions on the chain, any number of updates between them.

slides.title: A commitment that can be punished
slides.notes: A commitment transaction must be punishable, otherwise a party could publish an old state. The delayed output has two spending paths: a revocation key that works at once, or a wait of 1,000 blocks. At 999 confirmations the delayed spend is refused and at 1,000 it is accepted. The revocation path needs both halves of the key, so one half alone fails. A cheater must therefore wait a thousand blocks, while the victim, who holds both halves after the revocation, can take the output immediately. It is example 10 of the Run slide code menu.

slides.title: An HTLC: a secret or the clock
slides.notes: A hash time lock contract, or HTLC, lets a secret claim a payment before a deadline, and lets the payer take the money back afterwards. In the example the receiver claims the output with the right secret and a signature. A wrong secret fails the hash check whoever signs, and the payer's key cannot claim it. The payer's refund becomes final only at the lock height, nineteen blocks after funding. HTLCs are the building block that Lightning uses to route a payment across many channels, which the next part shows. It is example 11 of the Run slide code menu.

slides.title: The Lightning Network
slides.notes: The Lightning Network is the fourth part. It links payment channels end to end so that anyone can pay anyone through intermediaries, and every relay keeps a small fee for forwarding. The three columns name the three ideas of the part: routing and fees, onion routing in which the sender wraps the path in layers and each relay peels exactly one, and invoices together with the BOLT standards that let different programs work together. Every number in the code slides comes from the recorded run of five lnd nodes or from the specifications.
slides.new_title: The Lightning Network: payments across channels

slides.title: The Lightning Network: key concepts (1 of 3)
slides.notes: This slide defines 6 concepts of the part "The Lightning Network". BOLT: Basis of Lightning Technology: the numbered specifications that let different programs work together. Basic Lightning Network Example: Alice pays Eric one bitcoin through Bob, Carol and Diana, who each keep a small fee. Lightning Network: A network of payment channels that routes payments with hash time locks and onion packets. Lightning Network Benefits: Privacy, fungibility, speed, granularity, capacity and trustless operation. Lightning Network Transport and Pathfinding: Nodes talk over encrypted links, share channel news by flooding, and the sender plans the path. Routed Payment Channels (Lightning Network): Many channels linked end to end, so that anyone can pay anyone through intermediaries. Retell each in your own words and connect it with the example slides of the part. The chapter text and the course page explain them in full.

slides.title: Five nodes, one payment
slides.notes: This example follows one payment through three relays. Alice pays Eric one bitcoin, and Bob, Carol and Diana each ask 100,000 satoshis for forwarding. Each hop forwards what the later hops still need, so the surcharge over one bitcoin is 200,000 satoshis at Bob, 100,000 at Carol and nothing at Diana. Alice pays 300,000 satoshis in fees in all, and the library, which works backwards from the last hop, gets the same numbers. The chart shows the amount forwarded at each hop. Compare this with the fee concepts of chapter 9. It is example 12.

slides.title: Satoshis passed from hand to hand
slides.notes: This true story shows Lightning carrying real value for the first time as a game. On 19 January 2019 the pseudonymous Twitter user hodlonaut began a promotional test by sending 100,000 satoshis to a trusted recipient. Each recipient added 10,000 satoshis, worth 34 cents then, and sent the sum on; Jack Dorsey, Charlie Lee, Elizabeth Stark and Changpeng Zhao took part. Each hand-over was an ordinary Lightning payment, with no transaction on the chain for each step, which is the point of the second layer. The slide links to the original thread.

slides.title: The Lightning Network: key concepts (2 of 3)
slides.notes: This slide defines 5 concepts of the part "The Lightning Network". Sphinx: The packet format of the Lightning onion: fixed in size, with a check value for every hop. capacity: The sum locked in a channel; a payment must fit in the balance on the sending side. fee: A relay earns a fee for locking its funds while the payment is in flight. invoice: A payee's request for payment that carries an amount, a payment hash and an expiry. onion routing: The sender wraps the path in layers, and each relay peels one and sees only the next hop. Retell each in your own words and connect it with the example slides of the part. The chapter text and the course page explain them in full.

slides.title: Each hop has less time
slides.notes: A relay must always be able to reclaim its money upstream after it pays downstream, and time locks guarantee that. Every hop's HTLC expires at a block height, and the earliest expiry is at Eric's end. Neighbouring hops differ by 80 blocks, so a relay that pays downstream and then learns the secret still has time to claim from upstream; the last two hops share one expiry. The library rebuilds the same heights from the last hop backwards. The chart shows the blocks left on each hop. It is example 13 of the Run slide code menu.

slides.title: A paper that became a network
slides.notes: This true story records how a design on paper became a network. Joseph Poon and Thaddeus Dryja published the Lightning Network white paper in February 2015, describing a decentralized system for instant, high-volume micropayments that removes the risk of trusting third-party custody. It took years, soft forks and four independent teams before Lightning Labs launched the network in 2018. The picture shows its cut nodes growing from under 100 in 2018 to about 1,500 in 2022, read approximately from the chart. The book says the network was first described in 2015; the word proposed no longer holds.

slides.title: The Lightning Network: key concepts (3 of 3)
slides.notes: This slide defines 2 concepts of the part "The Lightning Network". pathfinding: Choosing a route with enough capacity and low fees, using the channel announcements. route: The chain of channels from payer to payee that a payment will follow. Retell each in your own words and connect it with the example slides of the part. The chapter text and the course page explain them in full.

slides.title: A hold invoice keeps a payment waiting
slides.notes: A hold invoice keeps a payment waiting in flight. Eric held back the secret, so the payment stayed pending along all four channels: one HTLC at each end and two at each relay, as the chart counts. When Eric cancelled, every balance returned to where it began. A later payment of the same kind settled once the secret was released. This shows that a Lightning payment is either claimed in full or returned, the property called atomicity, and that a pending payment holds balances in the channels it crosses. It is example 14 of the Run slide code menu.

slides.title: The encrypted link of BOLT 8
slides.notes: Lightning nodes talk over an encrypted link defined in BOLT 8, the eighth Basis of Lightning Technology document. The specification prints a test vector with fixed keys. The code reruns the handshake and compares the three outputs, the two acts and the transport key, with the printed values; every output is equal, so the handshake is implemented as specified. Acts one and three are 50 and 66 bytes, and the first message is 39 bytes. This is conformance by test vector, the same method used for signatures in chapter 8. It is example 15.

slides.title: The onion has a fixed size
slides.notes: Lightning uses onion routing so that no relay learns the whole path. A BOLT 4 packet holds a version byte, a key, 1,300 bytes of hop data and a check value, which makes 1,366 bytes whatever the route. The limit is twenty hops, and the hop data is padded, so a short route looks like a long one and a relay cannot tell how far it is from the end. The table lists the parts and their sizes. Connect this slide with the privacy benefit named on the concept cards. It is example 16 of the Run slide code menu.

slides.title: An invoice carries the hash
slides.notes: An invoice tells the payer what to pay and which hash will release the payment. A node on a private chain made an invoice for 100,000,000,000 millisatoshis, and the library parsed it. It asks 80 blocks for the last hop, and the secret, hashed once, equals the payment hash printed in the invoice. The invoice printed in BOLT 11 is dated 1 June 2017, and the prefix names the chain: lnbcrt is regtest and lnbc is the main chain. This links the invoice back to the HTLC of slide 30. It is example 17.

slides.title: A channel on the chain
slides.notes: A Lightning channel touches the chain only twice, and this example shows it. A channel is opened by one funding transaction and closed by one more. The funding output is a two-of-two script, and the closing transaction pays two taproot outputs. Six updates happened off the chain in between, and the chain never saw them. The table lists the two transactions and their outputs. This is the summary of the payment-channel part in code, and it ties back to slide 28. It is example 18 of the Run slide code menu.

slides.title: A breach and its punishment
slides.notes: A channel must punish cheating, and this example shows it end to end. Irene went back to an old state and published it. Hitesh's node saw the breach, and its justice transaction took the whole channel, although the last state owed Hitesh only 700,000,000 satoshis. A second test showed that a parent transaction with no fee can be lifted into a block by a child that pays for both, a technique called child pays for parent. Connect this with the revocation key of slide 29 and with watchtowers in the further reading. It is example 19.

slides.title: The chapter in five lines
slides.notes: These five lines are the deck in miniature, one for each part of the chapter and one for the idea that joins them. A line that feels unproven should send you back to its code slide, because every figure in it was computed there. The first line gathers the guarantees of the chain, the second colored coins, the third the two transactions of a channel, the fourth the revocation key and the HTLC, and the fifth routing with fees and falling time limits. The Run slide code menu reruns all nineteen examples.

slides.title: Where to go from here
slides.notes: This slide collects where to go next, grouped into reading, standards and papers, and tools. The Optech topics explain hash time locked contracts, anchor outputs and watchtowers with links to code. The BOLT documents are the numbered specifications that let different Lightning programs work together, and the white paper by Poon and Dryja is the original design. Blockchain explorers let you look at real channel opens and closes. Every entry is a live link in this file, and the course page lists the same sources with a short description of each.

slides.title: What you should now be able to say
slides.notes: This closing slide asks you to say each of four statements in your own words: what the chain guarantees, how a channel moves value off the chain, how a secret and a clock settle a payment, and how Lightning routes payments and punishes cheats. If one of them is hard, return to the slide named in the summary and run its code on the course page. Then compare your answers with the seven questions at the start of the deck. The book's chapter 14 and the sources on the resources slide are the next step.
